svg.text: DeepLearning.AI × Snowflake — Lesson 1 · turning audio, images, and video into searchable text
Audio, images, and video carry rich meaning. Turn each one into text with ASR, OCR, or a Vision Language
Model (VLM); embed the text as vectors; then your familiar SQL, search, and RAG stack works on all of it.
🎯 The challenge that just landed on your desk
One morning someone dumps a thousand new files into your data lake. They are not CSV or JSON.
They are audio recordings, images, and video clips. The message from a colleague is short: make it
searchable, add analytics on top, and turn it into RAG. Can you build that pipeline?
🧱 The familiar pipeline still applies — but the input has changed
Data engineers have shipped structured pipelines for years: load CSV / XML / JSON into tables, query
with SQL or Python, deliver insights. Same architecture works for unstructured data — once we can
turn audio, images, and video into something a table can hold.
🔹 Why multimodal data matters — what is hiding inside each file
Each modality carries far more than its surface. An audio file is not just a sound wave; an image
is not just pixels; a video combines everything. That richness is what makes it both valuable and hard.
💬 “Data is food for AI, and AI is hungry for context.”
💎 The size of the gap — most of your data has never been touched
A recent industry stat: more than 80% of enterprise data is unstructured (audio, images, video).
Less than 1% of it is ever processed or analyzed — not by AI, and not by anyone. That gap is the
untapped resource this course is about.
📜 Old reliable: ASR and OCR both convert rich data to text
Two well-known techniques shrink the gap. Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) turns speech into
written text. Optical Character Recognition (OCR) reads text out of slides, scans, and screenshots.
Both have improved dramatically thanks to deep learning. The key idea: once it is text, your
familiar SQL / table / search tools all apply.
🧠 Vision Language Models — comprehension, not just labels
Traditional computer vision answers what objects are in the picture: "person", "laptop". Useful, but
limited. A Vision Language Model (VLM) answers what is happening — it understands the scene and
writes a sentence about it. And, like ASR and OCR, the output is text, so the same downstream
RAG / SQL pipeline works on video too.
in the frame, not what is happening.
🧮 Embeddings — turn meaning into numbers so you can search by sense, not by keyword
If someone asks "when was the budget discussed?" but the meeting only talked about "financials",
keyword search misses it. An embedding is a vector — a long list of numbers — that places similar
meanings close together. Meeting text uses hundreds or thousands of dimensions so subtle
differences in meaning still have room to live in the space.
📐 Cosine similarity — search by angle, not raw distance
Once you have embeddings, semantic search becomes geometry: embed your query, embed each
document, and find the closest. The standard measure is cosine similarity, the cosine of the angle
between two vectors. It is fast and cheap to compute, which makes it scale.
🏗️ What you will actually build in this course
An end-to-end pipeline over the AMI Corpus — real product-design meetings with audio recordings,
slide images, and full video. Each modality runs through its own transform into text, all of it gets
embedded into a single vector store, and a RAG interface lets you query across everything.
📡 2026 intel — what teams actually reach for today
Curated picks for each layer of this pipeline as of mid-2026. Treat as starting points, not gospel.
Snowflake offers all of it natively.
Every modality you can turn into text is one more data source your existing RAG stack already handles.
The old bottleneck was perception — ASR, OCR, and now VLMs have made it good enough to industrialize.
